MINUTES OF THE MORNING SESSION

TUESDAY, APRIL 19. 1938
Iota Lodge. Kenyon College
Gambier. Ohio
The Convention was called to order at 10:30 A.M. by President
Collins. After the Chapter Roll had been called, the Recorder read the
minutes of the afternoon session of the previous day.
Motion was duly made, seconded and passed that the minutes of that
session should be approved as read.

A. Northey Jones, Beta Beta '17 (a member of the Executive Council
and its Treasurer), read the annual report of the Treasurer of the Execu
tive CouncU.
On motion duly made, seconded and
passed, this report was accepted
and referred to the Committee on Annual Communications.
Oral Chapter Reports were then continued by the senior delegates
present from the following Chapters :

Omega Tau Omicron
Pi Mu Delta Delta
Chi Rho Theta Theta

to the delegates.

On motion duly made, seconded and passed, it was voted to adjourn
the Convention untU 2:30 P.M., April 19.
The Convention adjourned at 12:40 P.M.

MINUTES OF THE AFTERNOON SESSION

TUESDAY, APRIL 19, 1938

Iota Lodge, Kenyon College

Gambier, Ohio
The Convention was called to order by President Collins at 2 :30 P.M.
After the Roll Call of the Chapters, the Minutes of the Morning
Session were read by the Recorder.
Motion was duly made, seconded and passed that the Minutes of the
Morning Session should be approved as read.
The Report of the Committee on Unfinished Business was read by
R. H. Pickford. Jr., Rho '38. It follows :

Resolved that:
1. The various Chapters in determining Chapter policy, give pri
mary consideration to the objectives of the Colleges with which the
Chapters are associated.
2. The Convention expresses gratification at the progress made
at Dartmouth College in this period of stress and recognizes the
excellent work of the Zeta Chapter in this progress.
3. The Convention appreciates the fine work of the Alumni Asso
ciation of Psi Upsilon under the leadership of Benjamin T. Burton,
Chi '21.
4. The Committee recommends that General Resolution No. 6,
as adopted at the 1937 Convention, applying to the improvement of
scholastic standing, be earnestly adhered to by the various Chapters,
and that a copy of this resolution be forwarded by the Executive
Council in each September to every Chapter.
5. The Convention recognizes and appreciates the work of Albert
C. Jacobs, Phi '21, in relation to his work on The Diamond and Psi
UpsUon Epitome and hereby sets the date of January 1, 1939. as the
deadline for all Chapter histories.
6. That each Chapter submit the name and address of its Fall
Rushing Chairman to the Executive Council by May 1. 1938.
7. That the requirements of the status relating to Federal Social
Security and Old Age Benefit Acts and to State Unemployment
Compensation laws as affecting each of our Chapters be immediately

checked with a legal authority to the end that no question of in
curring penalties may arise.
(a) The Convention recognizes and highly recommends the
investigation of Francis N. Bangs. Lambda '10 (a member of the
Executive Council), dealing with the above-mentioned legislation,
to each Chapter for its consideration.

Iota Lodge, Kenyon College
Gambier, Ohio

After Roll CaU, the Minutes of the Afternoon Session of AprU 19
were read by the Recorder.

Upon motion duly made, seconded and passed, the Minutes were ap
proved as read.
The Committee on New Business read telegrams to be sent to Scott
Turner, Phi '02, President of the Executive Council ; Archibald Douglas,
Lambda '94; Hon. Owen J. Roberts, Tau '95; Charles P. Spooner, Rho '94;
Edward L. Stevens, Chi '99; Emmett Hay Naylor, Zeta '09, Zeta Zeta
(Hon.) '36; R. Bourke Corcoran, Omega '15; Albert C. Jacobs, Phi '21,
Editor of The Diamond ; and Mrs. E. M. Anderson, widow of E. Malcolm
Anderson, Iota '14.
The Report of the Committee on New Business is as follows :
1. Resolved: Inasmuch as a portrait of Richard Hovey, Zeta '85,
has recently come into the possession of Sydney E. Junkins, Zeta '87,
and as he feels that it would be fitting that this portrait of an Ulus-
trious Dartmouth alumnus should be in the custodianship of Dart
mouth College, and that this should be presented to Dartmouth College
by the Executive Council of the Psi Upsilon Fraternity, therefore be
it resolved that the Convention of Psi Upsilon in its 105th year,
assembled at Kenyon College, Gambier, Ohio, appreciates the thought
of Brother Junkins and the friendly gesture therein, and requests the
Executive Council, if it concurs, to advise the President oJE Dartmouth
College of this gift to the College with an expression in conformity
with Brother Junkins' ideas.
2. Resolved: That in view of the fact that the Alpha
Chapter,
formerly at Harvard University (listed on our Chapter Roll as in
active), embraced only members of the classes from 1851 to 1874
inclusive, and since the former Alpha Chapter has been inactive since
1873, and, as far as can be learned, none of its former membership
of approximately 179 men is living, if the Executive Council
concurs.

Page Nine

RECORDS OF THE CONVENTION

the name of the Alpha Chapter be eliminated from our Chapter Roll.

3. Resolved: Inasmuch as the Treasurer of the Executive Coun
cil has reported to the Convention that an assessment of seventy-five
cents per year instead of the present one dollar per year assessment
per undergraduate member of the Fraternity is sufficient to meet the
regular Convention expenses, twenty-five per cent of the annual Con
vention assessment of one dollar be put into a fund which shall be
equally divided between the three Far Western Chapters, namely,
Epsilon, Theta Theta and Zeta Zeta, to help defray the traveling ex
penses of their delegates to the Convention, except that when the
Convention is held with one of the above mentioned Chapters this sum
be returned to the Convention Fund.

4. Resolved: That Resolution No. 5, adopted at the Convention
of 1926, calling for the appointment by each Chapter of "an alumnus
as its representative with whom the Executive Council might have

contact the same as with the Active Chapter," be rescinded.

5. Resolved: That each Chapter annually, on or about October
1st. inform the Executive CouncU of the names and addresses of
officers of its Chapter Alumni Association.
6. Resolved: That the Constitution of the Fraternity be amended
by striking out the phrase "fifteenth day of February" in Article 11,
Section 3, and substituting for it "first day of March."
7. Resolved: That it be suggested that future oral reports by
the several Chapter delegates be strictiy limited to a brief presenta
tion of the problems which the several Chapters have encountered,
and of attempted solutions to these problems.

8. Resolved: That the 1939 Convention be held with the Kappa
Chapter at Bowdoin College, Brunswick, Maine, and that if this
Chapter cannot be our hosts the matter be referred back to the
Executive Council for settlement, with power.
9. Resolved: That the request of the
Epsilon Chapter that the
1939 Convention be held with the Epsilon
Chapter at the University of
California. Berkeley. California, be referred to the Executive Coun
cil, provided that the Kappa Chapter relinquish its right by order of
Chapter founding.
10. Resolved: That it be recommended to the 1939 Convention
that the 1940 Convention be held with the
Sigma Chapter at Brown
University, Providence, Rhode Island, which year wiU mark the
one hundredth anniversary of the
founding of the Sigma Chapter.
n. Resolved: That the Recorder be instructed to send tele
grams of greeting from the Convention to :
Scott Turner, Phi '02

Hon. Owen J. Roberts, Tau '95

lon Fraternity assembled in Convention in its I05th year as guests of
the Iota Chapter, Kenyon College, Gambier, Ohio, on April 18. 19 and
20, 1938, extend their hearty thanks to the Iota Chapter, its alumni
and their committees, for their cordial hospitality to the delegates
and other members attending the Convention.
13. Resolved: That we hereby acknowledge our indebtedness to
Kenyon College for its warm welcome and also for its generosity in
providing facilities for our meetings, luncheons, and accommodations.
14. Resolved: That the Recorder be instructed to write a letter
to Dr. Gordon Keith Chalmers, President of Kenyon College, thank
ing him for whole-hearted cooperation with those Brothers planning
theConvention, and for his delightful address of welcome at our

Monday morning meeting.

that the 1941 Convention be held with the Gamma Chapter at Amherst
College, Amherst, Massachusetts, which year will mark the one

hundredth anniversary of the founding of the Gamma Chapter.

Respectfully submitted.
Committee on New Business,
By Albert Bosson. Chi '39

On the reading of each separate resolution a motion was duly made, sec

There being no further business. President Walter T. Collins. Iota '03,
declared the Convention adjourned sine die.

THE ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
OF THE

EXECUTIVE COUNCIL
TO THE

1938 CONVENTION OF PSI UPSILON
HELD UNDER THE AUSPICES OF THE

EXECUTIVE COUNCIL AND THE IOTA CHAPTER
Gambier, Ohio
April 18, 19 and 20, 1938
The Executive Council heartily welcomes and extends fraternal greet
ings to the delegates of our twenty-seven chapters at this Convention held
in the one hundred and fifth year of our Fraternity.

For the success of our Convention we will be very greatly indebted to
the generosity and whole-hearted spirit of the Iota Chapter and to the openarmed hospitality of Kenyon College, which in a manner and to an extent
we believe to be without precedent in the history of college fraternities, has

made the delegates and members of Psi Upsilon the guests of the College for
this event. To the Iota Chapter, to Kenyon College, and to its President,
Dr. Gordon Keith Chalmers, who in large measure is personally responsible
for the invitation extended to Psi Upsilon, on behalf of the Fraternity the
Executive Council expresses its very deep thanks.

The Objective of College Fraternities :

As youare aware, the usefulness of national college fraternities has

been seriously questioned at Dartmouth, and that challenge has been
repeated by undergraduates elsewhere.
These, attacks usually are based upon the question of contributions
toward national expense, which in the case of certain fraternities are heavy.
Psi Upsilon points with pride to its annual dues of only four doUars per
undergraduate the lowest, it is believed, of any national fraternity. The

national expenses of Psi Upsilon have always been small because men of
affairs, who learned to love Psi Upsilon and its ideals as undergraduates,
have given cheerfully of their time without remuneration to further the
usefulness of Psi UpsUon for the continuing benefit of the men selected to
perpetuate our Chapters.
In view of these attacks upon national fraternities, however, it is indeed
fitting that we should meet as guests of the Chapter where Earl D. Babst

Iota-Phi '93. who after many years on the Executive CouncU, served our
Fraternity as the sixth President of the Executive Council from 1924 to
l$29, first learned to love Psi UpsUon and to realize that its badge typifies
so much that is genuinely worthwhile.

Last autumn The Executive Committee of The Interfraternity Dart
mouth Committee, on which Emmett Hay Naylor. Zeta '09. and Vice
President of the Executive Council, faithfully served, rendered a prelimi
nary report from which we have taken the following significant excerpts :

"The fraternity has no existence apart from the college, and so
it must express itself always in terms of the life of the college. We
believe that the best way to buUd up a chapter that will be valuable
to its own particular national fraternity, is to make it definitely valu
able to its college, and a great contributing force to the objectives of
the college. If a chapter is actively loyal to its college, and as such
has a keen sense of responsibility to the college, it will automatically
have a keen appreciation of any fraternity association which has been
helpful to it in establishing itself on the local campus. * * *
"When our chapters demonstrate such concern for the develop
ment of their members that, with joining a given chapter, a man

will have improved greatly his chances of deriving the full benefits
of what Dartmouth College has to offer him, fraternity life at
Hanover wUl be vital, and your committee's task will be done.
"The fraternity is an opportunity to serve youth. It is the obliga
tion of maturity to help youth to a richer and wholesomer self-
expression. It is the simple relation of brother to brother, with all
that that connotes. We must not overorganize this relation. We must
never lose sight of its fundamental
purposes."
One hundred and five years is too long for any organization to endure
unless its fundamental concepts are sound ; its purposes are worthy ; and its
traditions and ideals are faithfully adhered to. We believe that throughout
its history Psi Upsilon has steadfastly striven to measure up to the tests
laid down in the report of The Executive Committee of The
Interfraternity
Dartmouth Committee, and that only because its efforts have been attended
with a large measure of success has it
received recognition as a great
fraternity.
Psi Upsilon has
consistently sought to be represented only at institutions
where fine men assemble ; to select the best men there obtainable and then
;
to bring out and develop in them their highest qualities of character and of
mind, their capacity for leadership and for genuine and fine friendships.

The Year's Accomplishment:

Reports made to the Executive Council by its members through official
visits, as well as information gained from communications received from
the universities in which our Chapters are located, reveal a record of accom
plishment and of solid strength in which we may all take pride. The
finances of our Chapters are satisfactory, and the Executive CouncU is able
to report that generally the Fraternity is in excellent condition.
In an effort to raise scholastic standings, early in this college year the
CouncU forwarded to each of our Chapters a copy of General Resolution
No. 6 adopted at the 1937 Convention, with the request that an earnest
effort be made to comply with the suggestions contained in this Resolution.
We recommend that a copy of this Resolution, as it may from time to time
be amended in Convention, be forwarded by the Executive Council in each
September to every Chapter.
Many of our Chapters have achieved outstanding scholastic rankings
and other Chapters have made marked improvement during the year. On
the other hand, a few Chapters still have disappointingly low scholastic
rankings among the social groups on their campus. This is a phase of
chapter life which calls for persistent and intelligent effort.

Alumni Association of Psi Upsilon :

The gratitude of the entire Fraternity is due to the officers and Board
of Governors of the general Alumni Association for their faithful and
untiring efforts to further the interests of Psi UpsUon. The
increasing
number of dues paying members speaks eloquently of the fact that more
and more of our alumni are becoming aware of the worthwhUe nature of
the Association's activities, all of which are carried on without interference
with the proper field of Chapter Alumni Associations. In order that the
delegates may be more fully informed and thus cooperate in enlisting
further
support for the Association among the alumni of their Chapters and particu-

larly from those who graduate in 1938, we urge each of you to attend the
annual meeting of the Association to be held on April 19th, 1938.

The Diamond :

Under the able editorship of Brother Albert C. Jacobs, Phi '21, Profes
sor at Columbia Law School, the form and content of The Diamond this
year have been outstanding. Brother Jacobs has worked diligently to inject
news interest in each issue and marked progress has been shown in improv
ing the character of thepublication. In addtion, all this has been accom
plished by keeping expenditures within budget limits. The Fraternity is
indeed indebted to Brother Jacobs for his loyal and efficient performance
of a difficult task.
An able and experienced committee of alumni have been selected by
the Council at Brother Jacobs' request, and have contributed a number of
valuable suggestions to augment his efforts.

Chapter Histories :

As editor of the second volume of the Psi Upsilon Epitome, Brother
Albert C. Jacobs urges the early completion of chapter histories. A number
ofour Chapters have fallen down on this task and we recommend that this

Convention set a definite time limit for its performance.
The Chapter history should not be merely an undergraduate effort. The
President of the Chapter Alumni Association should promptly designate a
qualified alumnus to supervise the compilation. Further work on the
Epitome awaits the factual material the Chapter histories will reveal.

New Directories :

The Executive Council has not as yet found it feasible to undertake
the task of publishing a new directory. Due to the increased activities of
our Alumni Association and to other
factors, the clerical work at our head
quarters office has so multiplied that it no longer remained possible to depend
upon old fashioned methods and one clerical assistant. To solve this situa
tion, modern type office equipment is being purchased in conjunction with
the Alumni Association to the end that much of our work previously

performed by hand can hereafter be done by machinery. When the de
tailed labor of instaUing this equipment has been
completed, we will again
approach consideration of the desirabUity of publishing a new directory.

Federal Social Security and Old Age Benefit Acts :

At the request of the Executive Council, Brother Francis N. Bangs.
Lambda '10. a member of the Council, made an examination of the govern
ing statutes relating to Federal Social Security and Old Age Benefit Acts.
and to State Unemployment Compensation Laws as affecting each of our
Chapters, and a copy of his opinion has recently been dispatched to each
Chapter. The Executive CouncU urges upon each Chapter the desirability
of checking the facts relating to its obligations under these acts with officers
of its Alumni Association to the end that no question of incurring penalties
may arise.

Petitions :

The Executive Council has no petition for a charter to submit to the
Convention.

Alumni Representatives of the Chapters :

Resolution No. 5 adopted at the Convention of 1926 caUs for the
appointment by each Chapter of "an alumnus as its representative with
whom the Executive Council might have contact the same as with the
active chapter."
Few Chapters have continued these appointments and it is believed a
more orderly procedure for the contacts of the Executive CouncU with

alumni to be with tbe regularly elected officers of Chapter Alumni Asso
ciations.
It is, therefore, recommended that Resolution No. 5 adopted in 1926
be rescinded, and that each Chapter annually inform the Executive Council
of the names and addresses of officers of its Chapter Alumni Association.

Vacancies on the Executive Council:

It is with a deep sense of sorrow and personal loss that the Executive
Council to the Convention the deaths during the
reports past year of
Dr. George Henry Fox. Upsilon '67, and of Eugene S. Wilson, Gamma '02.
Both of these brothers had served long and with distinction on the CouncU.
Dr. Fox was its Honorary President and for several years Brother Wilson
was its Vice-President. In their passing the Fraternity has suffered an
irreparable loss, and in the death of Brother Fox has lost one of the
last few remaining brothers whose personal recollections and contacts
stretched back to the early years of Psi Upsilon.
We call attention of the Convention to the fact that the terms of
Brothers Henry Hill Pierce, Kappa '96; LeRoy J. Weed. Theta '01. and
A. Northey Jones, Beta Beta '17. expire with this Convention.
There also
exists a vacancy due to the death of Brother Wilson. It
is, therefore
incumbent upon the Convention to elect three brothers for the usual
terms'
of five years each, and one brother for a term expiring in 1940.

EXECUTIVE COUNCIL OF PSI UPSILON FRATERNITY

Report of the Treasurer

1938

There is presented herewith a comparative statement of the Net Worth
of the various funds of the Fraternity held by the Executive Council as of
AprU 16, 1938 and April 26, 1937. A list of the investments held by the
General Fund and Bridgman Fund, showing cost and present market value
is also presented.
The cash position improved during the fiscal year due not only to a
larger amount of cash held uninvested in the Bridgman Fund but also due
to the fact that the cash balances in each of the other three funds were

larger than a year ago. Receivables of |260 are due from two chapters
for life subscriptions to the Diamond for initiates. These two chapters
should pay these amounts before the Convention closes.
The unrealized loss on investments held in the two investment funds
was $12,438.37. This is a very bad situation and has grown worse during
the year due to the depressed condition of the security markets. If invest
ments were carried in the statement at market value instead of at cost, the
aggregate net worth of the funds of the Fraternity would work out as

$34,123.19 as of AprU 16, 1938.
The income and expense accounts of the various funds are self-explan
atory. It will be noted that considerable economy has been effected in the
printing of the Diamond, the printing costs having been reduced over $1,000
in comparison with last year. The total surplus of receipts over expendi
tures (each of the four funds showing a surplus) amounted to
$3,632.34.
Of this amount, $999 has been appropriated to writcrdown the Albert Poole
Jacobs MemorabUia collection from $1,000 to $1 on our books. Of the
surplus in the Diamond Fund, $1,000 has been transferred to the Bridgman
Fund. Inasmuch as the main source of income for the Diamond Fund is
life subscriptions to the Diamond, a larger aUocation of the life subscrip
tion moneys should be made to the Bridgman Fund which is the permanent
endowment fund for the Diamond but it was felt that $1,000 was all that
could be safely transferred.

Again the Treasurer wishes to reiterate that every effort is being made
to keep expenses and consequently chapter taxes at a minimum. Taxes
of $4.00 per man per year are low in comparison with taxes of other
fraternities. Due to the fact that there has been a surplus of
receipts over
